title: Is Nvidia Stock Cheaper Now That Its Multiple Has Fallen? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Many investors evaluate NVIDIA (NVDA) the way they evaluate any stock: the lower the price-to-earnings multiple, the cheaper the stock. That multiple, what investors pay for each dollar of profit, stood at 101.3 for Nvidia in mid-2023. Today it is 26.5. Does a multiple that has fallen this far mean you are getting a cheaper stock? Nvidia’s share price rose 398.7% from mid-2023 to October 23, 2026, excluding dividends. A single share now costs far more than it did, while each dollar of profit behind it costs far less. Over the same three years, the price went up and the multiple went down. Nvidia’s profit over the latest twelve months reached $193 billion, compared with $10.3 billion in the twelve months to mid-2023. That is 18.7 times as much profit in three years. The table below shows how profit and the multiple moved year by year. Net income is the reported total for the twelve months ending on the date shown. Change in a year compares that net income to the twelve months prior. Each price-to-earnings multiple divides the market value at the calendar quarter end paired with those twelve months by the net income for those twelve months; the final row uses the share price of Oct 23, 2026. Nvidia generates its sales mostly from one business: the Compute & Networking segment made up 89.6% of revenue in fiscal 2026. On the August 26, 2026 call, management said a surge in AI demand is driving a global infrastructure buildout, and that sustained strength in Blackwell drove sales to hyperscale customers. Not in the way the rule suggests. A better question is what investors were paying for when the multiple was high. Nvidia’s multiple peaked at 143.1 in early 2023, when twelve-month profit had dipped to about $4.8 billion. Profit today is about 40 times that. Investors paid the most for each dollar of profit when there was far less of it because they expected it to grow, and it did. Today, a buyer pays less for each dollar of profit than a buyer did three years ago. That earlier buyer was paying for growth that has since happened. The lower multiple partly reflects growth that has already arrived, so it is not by itself a discount. This follows the usual curve for a fast grower: the multiple is highest while the profit is still expected, and lower once it is here. Nvidia’s profit is still growing fast, and it is expanding faster than it did a year earlier. Profit rose 122.7% in the latest twelve months, compared with 63.4% the year before. Profit also grew faster than sales, which rose 83.4%. Nvidia’s multiple today sits above the S&P 500’s 22.9. When Nvidia reports in November 2026, the figure to watch is whether profit keeps growing near the latest year’s pace. title: GOOGL's $250B AI Chip Opportunity Takes Aim At NVDA — Beth Kindig Says Google Is Going After ‘One Of The Most Profitable Hardware Businesses’ - Stocktwits
content: Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) could be positioning its artificial intelligence chips as a serious challenge to Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), with third-party Tensor Processing Unit sales potentially becoming a major new revenue stream, according to IO Fund analyst Beth Kindig. In a note on Friday, Kindig said Google's advantage may not come from simply building a faster accelerator, but from attacking the economics of AI infrastructure, particularly the cost of running increasingly expensive AI workloads. She said Google’s AI story is about to change “not from advancements in AI software, but by going after one of the most profitable hardware businesses the tech industry has ever seen.” Alphabet’s Class A shares closed 1% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, while Nvidia shares fell about 0.6%. Kindig says the AI accelerator market is entering a new phase as Google moves its merchant TPU strategy from announcement toward commercial execution. Google recognized its first TPU-related revenue from third-party customers in the second quarter. The analyst noted that the focus is increasingly on cost per token now, as massive AI infrastructure spending puts pressure on Big Tech's free cash flow. Google's latest TPU 8t and 8i systems are designed to improve performance per dollar compared with the previous-generation Ironwood TPU. Kindig says TPU 8i can deliver up to an 80% improvement in performance per dollar, particularly for low-latency inference workloads, while TPU 8t offers up to 2.7 times better performance per dollar for training. The result could allow customers to process substantially more AI workloads for the same infrastructure spending. “Google’s greatest competitive advantage may not be building a faster chip than Nvidia, but rather in building AI infrastructure at a lower cost,” she added. Kindig believes that the bigger opportunity for Google could come from the company selling TPUs directly to third-party customers rather than exclusively deploying them through Google Cloud. She added that this would create a second revenue stream for Google while shifting much of the upfront infrastructure burden toward customers, including data centers, power, cooling and hardware. Anthropic is already expected to deploy a gigawatt of Ironwood TPUs in 2026, followed by 5GW of TPU 8i in 2027 and another 10GW in 2028, according to Broadcom's update cited by Kindig, who believes that this would create a significant revenue stream for the company. At the high end, that would represent a staggering acceleration for Google's chip business, potentially reaching the current run rate of its Search business in just a few years, the analyst noted. Google's threat to Nvidia also extends beyond inference. Kindig highlights TPU 8t's ability to scale to a 9,600-chip superpod with 2PB of shared HBM and 121 exaflops of FP4 compute. Google's Virgo Network fabric can then connect 14 such superpods, creating a domain capable of supporting 134,400 TPUs. The scale could become particularly important if Nvidia encounters further delays with its next-generation systems, potentially giving Google additional room to gain accelerator share, she added. Rubio said allowing additional Russian diesel onto global markets could help ease pressure on fuel prices and benefit the U.S. as well as other economies. “We recognize the impact of this war on the global economy,” Rubio said, calling Trump’s decision to temporarily permit additional energy supplies onto the world market “very wise.” “This will benefit not only us, though, of course, it will also help the U.S., but it is also an important factor given high diesel prices worldwide,” Rubio said. Rubio’s comments come a week after the Trump administration waived key measures targeting Russian exports and countries that buy Russian energy. He said the president could take 60 days to assess the economic impact before deciding whether to proceed. The measures under the Graham Act include tariffs on Russian goods and penalties targeting countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas. Russia initially agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the U.S., with additional shipments expected in November and beyond. Meanwhile, during an interview with state broadcaster Vesti, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow is prepared to supply the U.S. with whatever volume of diesel its partners want. “As much as our partners want, to be honest, from the volume that we will export. We can supply everything,” Novak. As Bitcoin (BTC) struggles to find bullish momentum with bearish sentiment prevailing, investor Mike Alfred is prepared to bet up to $1 million that the cryptocurrency will hit $100,000 again before it falls below $60,000. Alfred also forecasted a possible run to 200,000-300,000 over the next three to five years. Speaking with SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci on All Things Markets, Alfred said, "I'd be willing to bet up to a million dollars cash that it hits 100k before it hits 60." Alfred said he expects Bitcoin to hit $100,000 in the next two to four months - a short-term call he said was "not financial advice." He said the cryptocurrency may have already made its last move below $60,000, after falling to about $57,000 to $58,000 earlier this year. Artificial intelligence has become one of the biggest investment themes in markets, with companies pouring billions of dollars into chips, data centers, software and AI models. But according to Apollo Global Management Chief Economist Torsten Slok, the much-discussed AI payoff has yet to show up across most of corporate America. Slok argued in a note on Saturday that the gap between technology companies and the broader S&P 500 is becoming increasingly important for investors. While the Magnificent 7 are seeing stronger revenue per worker and expanding profit margins, the rest of the index has yet to show a comparable improvement. Slok’s data painted a sharp divide between the Magnificent 7 and the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Revenue per employee has climbed significantly for the Magnificent 7, reaching roughly $780,000 on an inflation-adjusted basis, while revenue per employee for the S&P 493 remains around $525,000. Slok noted that the same pattern appears in profit margins. Margins for the Magnificent 7 have climbed to nearly 30%, while margins for the S&P 493 remain around 10%. The economist highlighted that the bigger question is whether AI is translating into broader productivity gains. Slok’s productivity data shows no clear acceleration in total factor productivity growth despite the rapid adoption and investment in AI. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” he said. Slok added that this leaves the broader corporate sector facing a difficult question: if AI is supposed to transform business, when will that transformation show up in revenue, margins and productivity? Slok added that one reason the macroeconomic impact may remain limited is that AI spending itself is highly concentrated. According to the economist’s data, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of spending on model serving and inference, 99% of neocloud spending and more than 95% of spending tied to OpenAI and Anthropic. Even cloud computing spending is heavily concentrated, with the top 10% accounting for 95.7%. The concentration also extends to venture-backed companies. Among the top 1% of AI spenders, 80.4% are VC-backed, compared with just 13.1% among median AI spenders. Slok argues that this matters because mainstream corporate America may not need the newest and most expensive AI models, particularly if companies cannot translate them into higher revenue or margins. “As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited,” he said, while adding that the biggest test for AI is no longer what happens at the largest technology companies. “The AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7,” Slok said. NEAR Protocol’s (NEAR) price edged lower on Sunday, extending its slide from October highs, as Near One chief technology officer (CTO) Anton Astafiev said the network was better prepared than Bitcoin (BTC) for a “Black Swan” event in cryptography. On The Rollup podcast published Saturday, Astafiev said NEAR was "better positioned than many earlier blockchains, especially Bitcoin." He credited the network's original account design, which allowed it to "add more signing schemes any time." Astafiev said most blockchains must pick one signing scheme, and in case they needed to switch later, that would be “a massive, massive transition and maybe years of work.” "For us, it's like we just roll it out,” he said. Astafiev said the team was "already thinking about Black Swan kind of events in cryptography, like cryptographic disaster or cryptography becomes broken today." Responding to Ethereum (ETH) researcher Justin Drake's recent warnings about quantum computing, he said that he wasn’t opposed to the message, but that he was “arguing with the way it was delivered." Astafiev said preparing for such an event would not be simple. “It's not going to be easy. It's going to be quite a significant amount of work,” he said. Alex Shevchenko, CEO of Aurora Labs and Defuse Labs, the team behind NEAR Intents, said that user-owned AI “should be free.” He said NEAR Intents, the network’s cross-chain trading service, was “exactly the money-making machine” needed to fund it. Additionally, NEAR co-founder Illia Polosukhin said NEAR AI aims to offer “private, verifiable, and secure AI” for people and companies. He tied that goal to NEAR’s focus on privacy. “Blockchain was supposed to be private,” he said. “Satoshi just didn’t have technology to do it.” His comments came as NEAR slipped more than 11% in a month. NEAR’s price was down over 2% during the past 24 hours, amid broader market weakness.  On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around NEAR was in the ‘extremely bearish’ territory, while chatter around it stayed at ‘low’ levels over the past day. Artificial intelligence is becoming a financeable infrastructure asset class as companies increasingly turn to debt markets to fund data centers and AI hardware, according to IO Fund. Morgan Stanley data cited by IO Fund shows AI-related debt issuance reached $466 billion through September, up from $101 billion during the same period in 2025. Goldman Sachs puts the figure at $489 billion as of July 22, already above the $322 billion raised throughout 2025. Nvidia shares closed 0.6% lower on Friday, Oracle shares closed 0.5% higher, while CoreWeave shares fell more than 2%. IO Fund's analysis shows Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Oracle Corp. (ORCL) and CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) occupy different positions in the debt-funded AI infrastructure chain. Lenders fund borrowers such as Oracle, CoreWeave and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX), which use that financing to purchase chips from suppliers including Nvidia. The borrowers then rent compute capacity to customers, while suppliers collect payment when chips are delivered. For Nvidia, the financing surge is supporting chip purchases across the ecosystem, analysts at IO Fund said. Nvidia generated $127 billion in free cash flow over the 12 months ended July 2026, IO Fund noted. It also added that Nvidia has signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR targeting more than $500 billion in third-party capital. CEO Jensen Huang said Nvidia retains the option to backstop up to $125 billion across these structures. IO Fund also notes that borrowers pay Nvidia and other chip suppliers upfront while customer revenue arrives over multi-year contracts. “AI compute is becoming a financeable infrastructure asset class,” IO Fund said. For Oracle, the debt burden is already visible in its financials, IO Fund stated, while adding that Oracle reported $125.3 billion in notes payable and borrowings in the first quarter (Q1). This is over three times its $37.1 billion in cash and marketable securities. Quarterly interest expense rose 55% year over year to $1.43 billion. Oracle also has $288 billion of new data center leases that have not yet started, with terms of 15 to 19 years. IO Fund said Oracle is reportedly considering an investor-funded entity that would purchase chips and lease them to the company, keeping the debt with the separate entity until the leases begin. For CoreWeave, IO Fund's analysis points to the direct cost of financing rapid capacity expansion. The neocloud generated $2.6 billion in second-quarter (Q2) revenue while spending $9.4 billion on quarterly capex, most of which was financed by debt. CoreWeave's total debt reached about $35.6 billion, while FY2026 capex guidance increased to $35 billion-$39 billion. Its Q2 interest expense jumped 140% year over year to $640 million, and the company guided to $860 million-$940 million for the third quarter (Q3). “That means more than 25% of its revenue goes to servicing its debt,” IO Fund wrote. CoreWeave also has approximately $15 billion of total debt due through 2028, while some higher-interest debt carrying rates above 10% is due in 2030 and beyond. title: NVDA Logs Best Day In Over A Month: Burry Spotlights Partnership Blitz — Analyst Calls Full-Stack Strategy ‘Underappreciated’ - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. Its target still implies a 56% downside from Tuesday’s closing price. At that price, SpaceX’s $1.95 trillion market cap values its shares at 2.11 times Morningstar’s fair value estimate. “The company's aggressively lofty valuation implies investors will have to wait decades for earnings to grow into SpaceX's multiples,” Morningstar said. The firm acknowledged why Musk’s investors may look beyond near-term financial hurdles. “Loyal holders of companies run by Elon Musk have a very long time horizon and are often willing to look past interim milestones toward the prospects of big bets on moonshot projects and the grander vision on the horizon,” it said. It highlighted robust revenue growth and margin expansion as compute leasing deals ramp, but flagged aggressive buildout targets and the dependence of the launch and connectivity businesses on successful Starship commercialization. Morningstar recognizes SpaceX’s competitive strength even as it questions the valuation. “SpaceX has transformed the economics of space launch and dominates the market for lifting spacecraft into orbit, and it has a decade lead on most competitors in experience and payload launch volumes,” it said. SpaceX delivered an estimated 83% of the mass sent into orbit in 2025. Its low internal launch costs also support Starlink’s economics, with Morningstar estimating returns on invested capital in the mid-20% range for the launch and connectivity businesses, above its 9.3% estimated cost of capital. However, uncertainty over heavy AI investment limits SpaceX’s overall moat rating to 'Narrow'. Morningstar expects AI to generate a majority of revenue by the end of 2026. Morningstar forecasts successful reuse of Starship upper stages by late 2028, enabling multiple launches per week and lower launch costs. The stakes extend across satellite connectivity and orbital computing. “If Starship does not prove to be reusable, however, it would put the company’s economic moat and operational future in doubt, as its V3 Starlink satellites and proposed AI satellites don’t fit in Falcon rockets,” it said. Its $70 base case already assumes viable orbital data centers, with 60,000 computing satellites providing 13 gigawatts of capacity and generating $168 billion in annual revenue by 2035. In a more aggressive expansion scenario, annual orbital computing revenue reaches $200 billion, but excessive capital spending and falling rental rates leave SpaceX worth just $26 per share, marking an 84% downside. Shares of Lam Research (LRCX) tumbled about 8% to $242 in overnight trading late on Wednesday despite record fiscal first-quarter results, as the chip-equipment maker disclosed supply constraints delaying some shipments and warned that China’s revenue contribution would fall in the December quarter. LRCX stock fell 1% to $260.81 on Wednesday, with shares on pace to log their third straight week of losses after dipping 1% so far this week. Lam reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion, beating the $8.14 billion consensus and setting a fifth consecutive quarterly record. Revenue increased 54% from a year ago and 22% sequentially, while adjusted EPS reached a record $2.20, above the $2.18 estimate. Gross margin improved to 52.4% from 52% in the June quarter. Operating margin climbed to 40.2% from 38.4%, crossing 40% for the first time. Memory systems revenue surged 120% year over year, while NAND revenue grew 40% sequentially. The Customer Support Business Group also delivered strong growth, with revenue rising 40% from a year earlier to nearly $2.5 billion. Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion and ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments, up from $5.6 billion in June. It repurchased $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends. The company has $3 billion remaining under its overall buyback authorization, with an accelerated repurchase program continuing into December. Its long-term goal remains returning 85% of free cash flow to shareholders. Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and adjusted EPS of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, versus consensus of $2.32. Gross and operating margins are expected to reach 52.5% and 40.5%, respectively, each plus or minus one percentage point. However, CFO Doug Bettinger said supply constraints limited the outlook. “I would mention that this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing,” he said. He declined to confirm an analyst’s estimated $300 million to $400 million impact, but said affected December shipments would move into March. CEO Tim Archer said some suppliers face demand growing faster than Lam’s own business. The company is working to expand supplier capacity and would consider investments if needed. “For those of us who were around during the COVID shortages, this is nothing like that. We learned a lot of lessons during that period,” Archer said. “I think we’ll be caught up very shortly.” Lam spent $258 million on capital projects and added about 1,900 employees during Q1. Inventory reached $4.6 billion, while inventory turns improved to a nearly seven-year high. The firm sees longer-term gross margins reaching the mid-50s. However, the adjusted tax rate rose to 16.5% from 11% in June and is expected to remain around that level in December and likely beyond. China accounted for 35% of September revenue, up from 26% in June, but Lam expects the share to fall substantially in December. “I expect that in December we’ll be meaningfully down, driven by the domestic customers in China,” Bettinger said. Multinational customers in China are expected to remain reasonably strong, although Bettinger did not quantify the overall decline. He also expects mature-node spending outside China to strengthen in 2027, with little meaningful growth this year. Lam expects AI demand to sustain semiconductor investment beyond the current supply constraints. “Our preliminary 2027 WFE outlook is for more than $200 billion of spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND,” Archer said. This compares with spending in the mid-$150 billion range expected for 2026. Lam sees demand through 2028 and 10 new major fabs opening in 2027. It also expects calendar 2026 systems revenue to grow well over 40%, marking a third consecutive year of industry outperformance. Foundry logic and DRAM have contributed 80% of systems revenue growth year-to-date. AI’s need for faster storage could further increase equipment demand. “Said differently, for each percentage point mix shift of NAND bits to SLC class devices, approximately 2% more installed wafer capacity will be needed to support the same bit demand,” Archer said. Lam raised its cumulative Aether-related revenue forecast through the decade’s end by $1 billion to $2.5 billion. Advanced packaging is expected to grow about 70% in 2026. “I would be stunned if advanced packaging didn’t grow nicely next year,” Bettinger said. Lam has shipped panel-plating systems to more than 20 customers and secured four backside-power tool-of-record wins at a leading customer. Archer also sees a shift to 3D DRAM increasing demand for Lam’s manufacturing processes. The support business is expected to grow more than 30% in 2026 and more than 15% in 2027, driven by upgrades, spares and services. Shares of Critical Metals Corp. (CRML) surged more than 8% in Thursday’s pre-market trade after the company announced a long-term rare earth supply agreement with REalloys Inc. (ALOY). REalloy shares were up nearly 6% in Thursday’s pre-market session. Critical Metals stated that under the agreement, REalloys will buy 15% of Tanbreez’s annual rare earth concentrate output. REalloys will also receive priority access to material with higher concentrations of dysprosium and terbium, along with a right of first refusal on additional volumes. The agreement builds on the Letter of Intent signed between the two companies in October 2025, converting the original 10-year framework into a binding 15-year contract with two optional five-year extensions. “This agreement marks a pivotal inflection point for Critical Metals and unequivocally validates Tanbreez as a world-class, development-stage asset of global strategic importance,” said Critical Metals Chairman Tony Sage. Critical Metals announced earlier this week that it had signed a definitive agreement to acquire European Lithium. Once the transaction completes, Critical Metals stake in the Tanbreez Rare Earth Project will increase to 100%, from the existing 92.5%. The agreement comes shortly after the Government of Greenland approved Critical Metals’ increase in ownership of the Tanbreez Project to 92.5% last month. Critical Metals held a 42% stake in the project prior to the government’s approval. Tanbreez is considered one of the world's leading heavy rare earth and critical minerals deposits, with substantial concentrations of dysprosium, terbium, and yttrium. These are key materials used in permanent magnets for defense, electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics, and advanced manufacturing. In December 2024, BlueOval SK was established by Ford, SK On, and SK Battery America to build and operate one battery plant in Tennessee and two in Kentucky. The Department of Energy agreed to finance the project and arrange up to $9.63 billion, with $7.84 billion advances subsequently made to the joint venture. In conjunction with the loan agreement, all the parties entered into a sponsorship agreement on December 13, 2024. Under this agreement, Ford guaranteed 50% of BOSK’s payment obligations of the BOSK DOE Loan. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, the plants would be able to produce over 120 gigawatt-hours of U.S. battery capacity annually. The statement also noted that the plants created more than 5000 construction jobs during the construction phase and will create 7,500 operational jobs as a part of the joint venture. This comes at a time when legacy automakers are prioritizing capital efficiency over aggressive EV expansion, as high battery costs and weaker EV margins weigh on profitability. Walmart expects earnings per share (EPS) in Q2 to be in the range of $0.72 to $0.74, below the $0.75 EPS that Wall Street analysts had expected, according to Fiscal.ai data. The company expects sales to rise between 4% and 5% and operating income to grow between 7% and 10%. U.S.-listed shares of Nio, Inc. (NIO) fell nearly 2% in premarket trading on Tuesday, even as delivery wait times for its flagship Nio ES8 dropped to just one to two weeks, although investors shifted focus toward the upcoming Nio ES9 rollout. Nio’s U.S.-listed stock fell over 1% in extended trading on Monday before rising marginally in the regular session. The sharp 92% decline in delivery timelines for ES8 comes after clearing over 100,000 firm orders accumulated after launch in September 2025, with new reservations now mostly aligning with production at the company’s Hefei manufacturing facility. The backlog normalization comes just weeks ahead of ES9 customer deliveries, which are scheduled to begin June 1, EV reported. Delivery timelines for the ES8 have narrowed steadily over recent months as production ramped and the company worked through its initial order pipeline. After debuting with a 24-26-week wait time in September, the timeline shortened to 13-14 weeks by January, then reached the current 1-2-week level by late April. Earlier incentive programs, including purchase tax subsidies, low-interest financing support, and free assisted-driving usage packages, have helped drive demand, but delivery timelines continued to decline. This was earlier flagged by Deutsche Bank as evidence that production was outpacing incoming demand. Some reservation holders are also apparently delaying purchases ahead of the ES9 rollout, mirroring the demand increases seen before the launches of other flagship models across the company’s lineup. The backlog clearance is a notable milestone since the ES8 has been one of the company’s most profitable anchors. Nio has previously said that the model carries a 20% gross margin, with an average selling price above 400,000 yuan ($5,862), implying a gross profit of 80,000 yuan per vehicle. Investor attention is now shifting toward the ES9, which opened pre-sales in April at a starting price of about 528,000 yuan and is expected to become the company’s next growth driver in the premium SUV segment. Deutsche Bank reiterated its ‘Buy’ rating on Nio’s Hong Kong-listed shares recently and raised its price target to HK$80 from HK$76, implying a 66% upside from current levels. The brokerage cited the ES9 ramp as a key contributor to improving operating leverage and stronger delivery expectations. The company also lifted its 2026 delivery forecast by 5% to about 420,000 vehicles and cut its projected full-year net loss by nearly half to 3.665 billion yuan. The transition between flagship cycles comes as the company continues moving toward its profitability target. The automaker reported its first profitable quarter earlier this year and is aiming to deliver its first full year of profitability in 2026, amid confidence in its premium-segment lineup. Nio’s first-quarter deliveries hit 83,465 vehicles, up 98.3% from the previous year and exceeding the upper end of the company's guidance. Meta Platforms, Inc.’s shares fell nearly 0.5% in early premarket trading on Tuesday. After news that Beijing had blocked the company’s acquisition of South Asian AI startup Manus, a new report said that the social media giant is moving to unwind the deal. Meta acquired Manus, which helps enterprises build AI agents, for $2.5 billion in December last year and quickly integrated its technology into its systems. Manus is headquartered in Singapore but has its origins in China. Meta is now preparing to unwind the acquisition, the Journal reported on Monday, citing people familiar with the matter. Earlier in the day, China said it was blocking the deal on national security grounds, according to a notice from the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China’s top economic planner. If true, unwinding the Manus deal would slow Meta’s push in the fast-moving agentic AI space. It also presents complications as around 100 Manus employees had already moved into Meta’s Singapore offices as of March, with founders taking on executive roles. “The transaction complied fully with applicable law. We anticipate an appropriate resolution to the inquiry,” a spokesperson at Meta told TechCrunch. Manus has yet to comment. According to the Journal’s reporting, Beijing has handed Meta and Manus a preliminary deadline of several weeks to unwind the deal and fully restore Manus’s Chinese assets to their original state. This includes stripping any previously transferred data or technology from Meta. Beijing has also considered imposing penalties on Manus and Meta if the deal couldn’t be fully rescinded. Several former Manus investors in Asia, including Tencent, HSG and ZhenFund, have planned to cooperate if Meta goes ahead to unwind the deal, some of the people said, according to the report. To be sure, Beijing had launched a review shortly after the deal was announced and, in March, called in Manus co-founders Xiao Hong and Ji Yichao for a discussion. The executives were later told not to leave the country pending the investigation, it was reported at the time. Manus’ founders previously established its parent company, Butterfly Effect, in Beijing in 2022 before relocating to Singapore. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for META was ‘bearish’ early Tuesday. Investors were broadly focused on the company’s quarterly report due on Wednesday. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences Group, Inc. (SLS) came into focus on early Tuesday after a portfolio manager, known for backing several “Magnificent Seven” stocks, increased its stake in the cancer drugmaker ahead of a survival-event trigger in its Phase 3 acute myeloid leukemia (AML) program. SLS stock jumped over 9% on Monday amid rising hopes around the database-lock milestone for Sellas’ Regal study, which could unlock topline survival data from its lead immunotherapy candidate, GPS. On Monday, Commonwealth Equity Services increased its stake by 32%, adding 9,226 shares to bring its total holdings to 38,470 shares valued at about $162,730 as of March 31. The boost in stake places Sellas among its other heavyweight healthcare bets, including Eli Lilly, Pfizer, and UnitedHealth. Among its larger portfolio, Sellas sits among its “Magnificent Seven” allocations, including Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon. Recently, BlackRock also disclosed ownership of 12.1 million shares, representing 6.8% of Sellas’ shares. Additionally, Dagco raised its position by 78% to 1.03 million shares valued at $4.35 million, making Sellas its second-largest allocation alongside healthcare holdings such as Merck, Thermo Fisher Scientific and Johnson & Johnson. The increase in stake comes after Sellas CEO Angelos Stergiou said late Sunday that his confidence in the Regal study’s commercial potential remains unchanged despite the trial remaining blinded. “My conviction in the REGAL trial’s prospects and ultimate commercial potential remains as steadfast today as it was day 1,” he said. The ongoing event-driven Phase 3 Regal study is evaluating GPS in patients whose acute myeloid leukemia returned but later entered remission following additional therapy. Final analysis is expected once 80 overall-survival events are recorded, which will trigger database lock, statistical analysis and unblinding. The company previously reported 72 survival events as of Dec. 26, bringing the study closer to the required threshold. Stergiou previously said that slower accumulation of survival events in oncology trials can sometimes indicate patients are living longer than initially expected. Beyond the Regal program, Stergiou also said investors should expect updates and topline data readouts from ongoing Phase 2 studies of the company’s CDK9 inhibitor SLS009 this year. Alongside pipeline progress, Sellas is seeking shareholder approval to expand its share reserve under its 2023 Amended and Restated Equity Incentive Plan by 20 million shares. The company said that only 7,991 shares are available for future awards under the existing plan as of mid-April. The approval would allow a previously approved grant of 1.1 million restricted stock units to Stergiou to take effect. If rejected, the award would automatically be canceled, and alternative compensation arrangements may be required. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SLS was ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volume. One user said, “Far more important than Blackrock or Vanguard is the fact that private wealth and family offices have been actively buying and hoarding shares. Lot of money in that segment. Careful but patient money.” Another user said, “The CEO must have already discussed this 20 million shares with huge partners. It wil pass. Retail is just making noise. The real players like blackrock will surely approve.” SLS stock has surged nearly 250% over the past year. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. title: China's Moonshot Reportedly Seeks Access To More NVDA Blackwell Chips A Week After Trump Official Flagged Export Control Breach - Stocktwits
content: Chinese artificial intelligence startup Moonshot AI is seeking access to more of Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) advanced Blackwell chips to train its next-generation Kimi K4 model. According to a report by The Information citing people familiar with the matter, Moonshot is planning a significantly larger successor to its recently launched Kimi K3 model. Nvidia shares edged up by 0.1% in Tuesday morning’s trade. The report said Moonshot trained its 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model using Nvidia chips, including advanced Blackwell GPUs, despite U.S. export restrictions that are intended to prevent Chinese companies from accessing the technology. According to the report, the startup is now looking to secure additional Blackwell chips to support development of K4, underscoring its continued reliance on Nvidia's cutting-edge hardware for training frontier AI models. The report added that Moonshot stitched together computing capacity from at least two Chinese cloud providers because no single supplier could provide enough Blackwell chips. Engineers also optimized networking across the separate data centers to improve communication between the GPUs during training. According to the report, Moonshot also relies heavily on Nvidia's H20 chips to run Kimi K3 on its platform. The startup reportedly recommends that customers hosting the model connect at least 64 server chips, while surging demand forced it to stop accepting new subscriptions within 48 hours of the model's launch because its GPU capacity was stretched. The report added that Beijing has discouraged local companies from using Nvidia's H20 chips in favor of domestically designed alternatives. However, the large AI servers needed to run frontier models using Chinese chips remain in limited supply, with customers reportedly facing delivery wait times of as long as six months. The report comes a week after Michael Kratsios, Assistant to the President and the thirteenth Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, alleged in a post on X that Moonshot had acquired Nvidia GB300-equipped servers and accessed GB300 systems in Thailand to train its AI models despite U.S. export controls. He also claimed the company developed a sophisticated platform to access U.S. AI models while avoiding detection. Kratsios further alleged that Moonshot used large-scale distillation of Anthropic's models to develop Kimi K3. While he said the U.S. supports legitimate AI distillation to create smaller and more efficient models, he argued that “large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U.S. technology and undermining American research is unacceptable.” NVDA stock is up 5% year-to-date and 11% over the past 12 months. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 16% over the past 12 months, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 19%. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) is up 27% during this period, while the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW) is up 28%. Shares of Replimune (REPL) crashed nearly 32% on Tuesday after its lead skin cancer therapy came under fresh scrutiny, with U.S. Food and Drug Administration staff reviewers stating the company has not provided clear evidence that the drug works as claimed. The concerns were outlined in briefing documents released ahead of an advisory committee meeting on July 30. A Final FDA decision is targeted for August 2. REPL shares have been under heavy selling pressure and are on track for a fifth straight day of losses, with the stock down about 47% during that stretch. The stock also fell below the 100-day (100-DMA) for the first time in nearly two months. Replimune is seeking approval for RP1 in combination with Bristol Myers Squibb’s immunotherapy Opdivo for patients with advanced melanoma. The company based its application on the IGNYTE study, which reported an objective response rate (ORR) of 33.6% and a median duration of response of 24.8 months. According to Replimune, some patients achieved complete disappearance of their tumors. However, FDA reviewers said the way tumor responses were measured using RECIST v1.1 criteria may have artificially inflated both the response rate and the duration of response. Because RP1 is injected directly into tumors, the agency said the shrinkage seen in treated tumors could reflect a local injection effect rather than a broader anti-cancer effect throughout the body. Another issue for the FDA is that IGNYTE was a single-arm trial, meaning all patients received the combination of RP1 and Opdivo and there was no comparison group receiving Opdivo alone. Without a control group, reviewers said they cannot determine whether RP1 contributed anything meaningful to the observed responses. The FDA also said the overall survival data submitted by Replimune cannot be reliably interpreted to show a treatment benefit. The latest review adds to a difficult regulatory history for Replimune. The FDA previously rejected the RP1 application in July 2025 and again in April 2026 through Complete Response Letters, before reaching an agreement with Replimune in May 2026. The agency had agreed to prioritize the review because of the significant unmet need in advanced melanoma. One user opined that swift FDA acceptance of an application is not an endorsement. Shares of PayPal (PYPL) gained in morning trade on Tuesday after the company reported a beat-and-raise second quarter, and CEO Enrique Lores stated the company is “open” to assessing buyout opportunities that come its way. PYPL stock gained over 2% in morning trade and was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around the company improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ territory over the past day, and chatter increased to ‘normal’ from ‘low’ levels. Platform data showed a 900% jump in message volume over the last 24 hours. PayPal, which reportedly received a $50 billion takeover proposal earlier this year, would “carefully consider” any future offers through the lens of shareholder value, Lores said. "We remain open and objective in evaluating opportunities," Lores said during the company's second quarter (Q2) earnings call on Tuesday. "And if we see levers or a path that we believe would create superior value for our shareholders than executing our current strategy, we would of course carefully consider them." PayPal reported second-quarter revenue of $8.7 billion, ahead of analysts' expectations of $8.47 billion, according to Koyfin data. Earnings per share came in at $1.25, topping the consensus estimate of $1.23. "I'm encouraged by the progress we made this quarter," Lores said. "We moved with urgency to sharpen our transformation plan and advance our growth strategies across our three businesses." He said branded checkout continued to stabilize, while Venmo and Braintree maintained strong momentum. The company is also expanding into financial services to diversify its business model. PayPal raised its full-year non-GAAP earnings outlook to approximately $5.38 per share, up from its previous guidance that ranged from a low-single-digit decline to slightly positive versus last year's $5.31. Tuesday's results come as PayPal continues a broad restructuring under Lores, who took over as CEO in March after previously leading HP. In May, the company announced plans to eliminate roughly 4,760 jobs, or about 20% of its workforce, over the next two to three years. The restructuring is expected to generate approximately $1.5 billion in annualized savings and is intended to fund investments in higher-growth areas of the business. PYPL’s stock has fallen over 1% this year and dropped over 25% in the last 12 months. Shares of Galaxy Digital (GLXY) failed to recover in morning trade on Tuesday despite the company announcing it bought around 500 acres in McGregor, McLennan County, Texas, for a second artificial intelligence and high-performance computing data center campus. GLXY stock fell over 10% during morning trade, to lows not seen since April, in tandem with the broader weakness seen within the crypto equity market. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around GLXY remained in the ‘neutral’ territory, while chatter around it shifted to ‘low’ from ‘normal’ over the past day. The firm announced a development agreement with the City of McGregor for the McGregor site to build and operate an AI and high-performance computing campus in the McGregor Industrial Park. The city collected some $7.5 million in revenue from the sale of the land. The first phase of development is expected to be 74 megawatts (MW), just below ERCOT’s large load threshold of 75 MW, with power expected to flow in 2028 pending completion of development milestones. Galaxy believes the campus has the potential to scale into a multi-hundred-megawatt facility through 2030. "The demand for compute is a structural shift, not a passing cycle, and we believe the right way to meet it is by building infrastructure that strengthens the communities that host it," said Mike Novogratz, Founder and CEO of Galaxy. Novogratz positioned McGregor as the next step in building a “disciplined, multi-campus data center business,” pointing to Galaxy’s Dickens County track record as proof that a privately funded campus can be a long-term economic partner to a rural community. Galaxy is the biggest employer and taxpayer in Dickens County. Galaxy’s acquisition of McGregor arrives as the company, like many others, broadens its pivot away from Bitcoin (BTC) mining toward AI and high-performance computing infrastructure. This campus marks Galaxy’s second big data center investment in Texas after its 1.6 GW Helios flagship in Dickens County that has become one of North America’s largest AI and HPC campuses. content: U.S. stock indices ended Monday lower as elevated Treasury yields continued to dampen the demand for riskier assets, while media reports suggested President Donald Trump was willing to provide Iran some sanctions relief. The S&P 500 ended Monday 0.8% lower, the Nasdaq 100 eased 1.1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.7%. The Russell 2000, which tracks stocks with small market capitalizations, fell 0.7%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.7%, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) slipped 0.6%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) fell 1%. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell between 1% and 2%, tracking weakness in Broadcom (AVGO) and Micron Tech (MU) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) slipped about 0.7%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for QQQ, SPY, and DIA was ‘bullish’ with ‘high’ message volumes. According to media reports from CNN and Axios citing White House officials, President Donald Trump expressed a willingness to offer Iran sanctions relief regarding nuclear issues, pulling crude prices down from their peak levels of the day. Meanwhile, Treasury yields continued their upward trajectory following last week’s substantial advance. The standard 10-year Treasury note yield pushed past 5.2%, as the 30-year bond yield surpassed 5.5%, leaving both hovering near multiyear peaks. Those yields have “come back up meaningfully today, and that’s causing an understandable weakness in the tape,” Justin Bergner, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told CNBC. “The competition for capital with AI hyperscaler spending ... also pressures the consumer with higher rates, so it kind of makes the market more one-sided than it already is.” Recent commentaries from Federal Reserve Governors and officials about soaring inflation amid elevated oil and heightened AI capex spending, and the need for more rate hikes to keep it under control, have caused U.S. yields to jump to their highest in over a decade. Efficiency improvements driven by artificial intelligence are unlikely to cool down near-term inflation, according to Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, who cautioned that heavy infrastructure spending in the sector may actually fuel short-term price increases. "Currently, I anticipate that productivity gains will provide modest disinflation within the next few years," Cook said. "However, I do not expect those effects to arrive in time to offset the broadening inflationary pressure later this year." Gene Munster, managing partner and co-founder of Minneapolis-based Deepwater Asset Management, said on Monday that SpaceX’s first orbital Starship flight was a bigger milestone than the stock reaction implied. Writing on X after the launch, he added that even investors who expected a good outcome were “underappreciating the significance” of the mission. SpaceX’s 14th Starship test lifted off from Starbase, Texas, and put the upper stage into Earth orbit for the first time. All 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites on board were released and later confirmed as operating. That was the first operational payload ever flown on Starship. It was not a clean flight. One of the six engines on Ship 41 shut down during the climb. SpaceX still completed the burn that put the vehicle into orbit, then cut the mission short. The plan had been about 10 hours and six loops around Earth. After the engine problem, the company brought the ship home after about three hours and a controlled splashdown in the Pacific. Munster framed the day as “double and quadruple good news.” First, “with the help of some rounding,” Starship is about twice the size of Falcon Heavy. Getting a rocket that large into orbit, he said, is a milestone because it should let SpaceX put satellites up cheaper and faster. Second, Starlink speeds “should about 4x with V3,” the first of which reached orbit on Monday. He said new pricing tiers are coming and that the average Starlink download should rise from about 150 Mbps to about 600 Mbps. SpaceX has said each V3 satellite is built for far more capacity than the smaller V2 Mini birds flown on Falcon 9, and that a full Starship load can add as much network capacity as many Falcon 9 missions. Monday’s flight carried 26 of a possible 60. Boeing (BA) shares fell about 7% on Monday, clocking its worst day since April 2025, as investors digested a fresh regulatory setback for the company’s biggest 737 Max 10 variant jet. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is delaying certification of the 737 Max 10 variant because of a newly flagged software issue, just as Boeing appeared close to winning approval to start delivering the jet, Bloomberg reported. According to the report, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters at an event near Washington that the agency will wait until it decides whether the glitch is a “safety of flight” concern. He added that approval will wait until the FAA is “satisfied that we don’t have an issue here.” The Wall Street Journal first reported the underlying problem on Saturday, citing Boeing documents. The Journal said an update to the flight-management computer can drop automated vertical navigation after a missed approach if the crew changes the planned path. In that narrow case, pilots may have to fly more themselves at low altitude. Boeing reportedly told operators in August that the issue was not an immediate safety risk and said it had reminded airlines of existing procedures. A lasting software fix had been slated for 2028; the company now says it is trying to move that work up. The glitch is tied to flight-management software versions 14 and 14.1. The recently certified Max 7 used version 14. The Max 10 used 14.1 in certification testing. Southwest and United have told Boeing they do not want new jets with the affected software and would rather take an earlier version, the Journal reported. Several U.S. airlines said their in-service Max fleets do not use those builds. The FAA said over the weekend it was reviewing the issue. The jet was previously expected to be certified in the coming weeks. The Max 10 is the largest jet in Boeing’s best-selling single-aisle family and has been years behind schedule. Flight testing finished in July. As recently as last week, Alaska Airlines, one of the large customers, still thought certification could come within days. The smaller Max 7 was certified in August, with first deliveries also hanging in the balance if regulators treat the software as a safety issue. The jet accounts for roughly 30% of Boeing’s undelivered 737 orders. Firm Max 10 orders have been cited in the 1,400-to-1,500 range. Starting deliveries would let Boeing begin converting a large slice of that backlog into cash. (AMD) on Monday announced the purchase of artificial intelligence startup World Labs in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $8.2 billion, aiming to strengthen its position against rival Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) The transaction is expected to close by year-end, subject to standard regulatory approvals. AMD stock eased about 4% on Monday, while NVDA stock gained about 1.8%. Founded by renowned Stanford University researcher and computer scientist Dr. Fei-Fei Li, World Labs brings together roughly 70 specialists and software expertise focused on spatial intelligence and “world models.” The startup develops software that can generate, reconstruct, and simulate interactive three-dimensional physical environments. These systems serve as foundational frameworks for advancing autonomous robotics, manufacturing automation, and complex scientific research. As part of the definitive agreement, Li will join the chipmaker as executive vice president and chief scientist, directly reporting to AMD Chief Executive Officer Dr. Lisa Su. "The more you understand end to end, the better system you are going to build," Su said in an interview with Bloomberg Television. "That’s why we are acquiring World Labs—to have access to the world-class talent Fei-Fei has brought together and bring it together with AMD’s capabilities around hardware, software and systems." The acquisition aligns with AMD’s broader strategy to deliver comprehensive data center offerings, combining chips, infrastructure, and software capabilities. The enterprise client market remains AMD's primary revenue driver as tech infrastructure expands to support next-generation artificial intelligence applications. Li noted that the venture's expanding ambitions required access to significantly greater computing infrastructure. "At this point, if we can join forces with AMD, we really are giving ourselves, AMD and the ecosystem an opportunity to accelerate the flywheel between software and hardware development," Li said. The acquisition comes during an intensive period of dealmaking across the semiconductor and artificial intelligence sectors. Market leader Nvidia recently agreed to acquire open-source platform Hugging Face in a deal valued at $13 billion. While AMD remains second to Nvidia in the market for specialized AI accelerator chips, investor enthusiasm for its execution has surged, pushing the company's valuation to roughly $1 trillion. Integrating World Labs' spatial AI architecture is expected to help refine future hardware designs and expand the company's range of open and proprietary AI model offerings for enterprise clients. (NVTS) shares jumped 20% in after-hours trading on Monday after the company said it had been selected for a U.S. Army-sponsored program to develop ultra-high-voltage silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductor technology. The program's financial terms were not disclosed. At the time of writing, NVTS shares had pared some of their after-hours gains but were still trading 14% higher. Earlier, the stock ended the regular session 3.85% lower. The company was awarded the ALATTIS program, which stands for Accelerated, Large-Area, 10 kV SiC IGBT. The initiative will focus on developing next-generation 10 kV silicon carbide power semiconductor technology. The Army selected Navitas following a competitive evaluation involving leading U.S. silicon carbide technology companies. Navitas said the selection recognized its work in ultra-high-voltage SiC innovation, its ability to deliver defense-grade performance and reliability, and its U.S.-anchored manufacturing ecosystem for advanced power semiconductor technologies. The ALATTIS prototype project will develop, execute, and validate a domestic manufacturing process for ultra-high-voltage SiC power semiconductor devices. The work will use an iterative process involving design, fabrication, and testing. The program is sponsored by the Army Research Laboratory, which operates under the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command. The initiative aims to develop 10 kV SiC insulated-gate bipolar transistors and related PiN diode technologies for mission-critical systems used by the Armed Forces. Navitas’ GeneSiC silicon carbide portfolio covers voltage ratings ranging from 650 V to 6.5 kV and is manufactured through a U.S.-anchored supply chain. The company has also developed several ultra-high-voltage SiC technologies over the years, including 6.5 kV SiC thyristors in 2010, 10-15 kV PiN diodes in 2012, and 6.5 kV SiC MOSFETs in 2021. Efficiency improvements driven by artificial intelligence are unlikely to cool down near-term inflation, according to Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, who cautioned that heavy infrastructure spending in the sector may actually fuel short-term price increases. Speaking at an event in Oakland, California, Cook noted that while AI promises long-term economic gains, its immediate cost impact presents challenges for monetary policymakers. Cook projected that productivity enhancements from AI would provide only minor disinflationary relief in the coming years, which is too late to curb the broader price growth expected in the near term. "Currently, I anticipate that productivity gains will provide modest disinflation within the next few years," Cook said. "However, I do not expect those effects to arrive in time to offset the broadening inflationary pressure later this year." She characterized AI as potentially "the most significant technological shift of our lifetime," but emphasized that significant uncertainty remains regarding how fast those efficiency gains will materialize. Rather than curbing inflation, the current AI expansion is contributing to cost pressures through intensive infrastructure spending. Extensive investment in data centers has intensified competition for shared resources, including construction labor and energy supplies. This demand spike has already driven up electricity and water expenses by approximately 5% over the past year. With corporations having spent only a fraction of an estimated $2 trillion in pledged capital, alongside AI-fueled stock gains that boost consumer spending, Cook cautioned that wider inflationary risks remain prominent. The central bank recently voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point, with projections pointing toward at least one additional rate hike before the year ends. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh indicated the decision was intended to reduce economic accommodation and move inflation back toward the 2% target. Financial markets reflect an increased likelihood of continued policy tightening, with federal funds futures pricing in roughly a 70% probability of an October rate increase. Cook expressed confidence that the economy can absorb further rate hikes, citing low unemployment and broad economic resilience. She noted that the labor market remains balanced, improving, and well-positioned to handle additional policy adjustments. title: This NVDA Partner’s Stock Jumps 7% — Why UBS Sees 38% Upside For Amkor Technology - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Amkor Technology Inc. (AMKR) rose more than 7% in morning trading on Friday after UBS upgraded the semiconductor packaging and testing company to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral,’ citing stronger long-term growth driven by artificial intelligence demand. The investment bank also raised its price target to $90 from $80, implying nearly 38% upside from Thursday’s closing price. UBS said Amkor’s recently expanded $1.5 billion strategic partnership with Nvidia (NVDA) supports the company’s growing role in packaging the chipmaker’s next-generation AI processors, including the Vera CPU, GB10, N1X and future products. The firm also sees an opportunity for Amkor to accelerate its business related to Advanced Micro Devices' Venice CPU as demand continues to improve, according to CNBC. On Thursday, Amkor expanded its multiyear advanced chip packaging partnership with Nvidia through a $1.5 billion agreement that includes a cash prepayment. The partnership is designed to accelerate the development of next-generation AI hardware and expand domestic chip processing capacity in the U.S. UBS expects Amkor to add $1.1 billion in advanced packaging revenue in 2027. The firm said the company’s advanced packaging business should benefit from rising server CPU volumes, growth in its base business, tighter capacity and price increases to offset inflationary costs. Earlier this year, Amkor signed a 10-year agreement with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. It also maintains an ongoing business relationship with Advanced Micro Devices. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AMKR improved to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ in the past 24 hours, while message volume was ‘extremely high’ at the time of writing. Over the past seven days, message volume around the stock has surged 940%, while the ticker's retail watcher base jumped 2.6% in the same period. Amkor shares have gained nearly 62% year to date as the AI boom has fueled demand for advanced chip packaging. Shares of MannKind Corporation (MNKD) jumped 8% on Friday after the company said that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Furoscix ReadyFlow, a simple autoinjector designed to treat fluid buildup, known as edema, in adults with heart failure or chronic kidney disease. The device is the first and only autoinjector that delivers a treatment equivalent to an 80 mg/mL dose of subcutaneous furosemide. Patients or caregivers can use it at home in under 10 seconds, with relief often starting within an hour. This offers patients an earlier option to manage worsening symptoms and may help avoid emergency visits or hospital stays. According to MannKind's estimates, about 6.7 million U.S. adults live with heart failure, a number expected to exceed 8 million by 2030. Fluid overload drives many of the symptoms and high costs linked to the condition, which often occurs alongside chronic kidney disease. The product builds on an earlier version of Furoscix already available and is expected to reach the market by the end of August 2026. Furoscix’s last recorded revenue was $15.5 million in net sales for the first quarter of 2026. Alongside the approval, MannKind announced it has entered into a securities purchase agreement for a private placement expected to raise approximately $50 million in gross proceeds from institutional investors, led by Frazier Life Sciences. The company plans to use the funds for general corporate purposes, including a $45 million payment to former shareholders of scPharmaceuticals, as part of MannKind’s October 2025 acquisition of the company. The payment was triggered by the FDA approval. title: Apollo finds no broad AI payoff: NVDA stock forecast before earnings - Techi
content: Apollo sees little AI payoff beyond big tech. TECHi finds Nvidia’s EPS estimate held steady while NVDA’s forward multiple fell 6%, then maps conditional prices before earnings. Illustrative data-center racks, not a verified NVIDIA facility. Photo by Brett Sayles / Pexels, used under the Pexels License; cropped and toned by TECHi. Apollo's chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence. That is a warning about the economics of the buyers at the far end of the AI chain, not a new earnings report from Nvidia. For NVDA holders, the immediate question is whether the market will lower the price it pays for Nvidia's expected earnings before those earnings themselves turn down. There is already a measurable gap. From September 24 to the October 23 close, TECHi's NVDA forecast data show the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124, while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculates a 0.06% estimate increase against a 6.06% price decline. The implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65. That compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, is the starting point for this forecast. Our calculation uses two dated observations of the same fiscal-year EPS estimate and the corresponding daily closes. The September 24 observation shows $224.58 divided by $9.3071, or 24.13 times. The October 23 close of $210.96 divided by $9.3124 yields 22.65 times. The ratio fell roughly 6.12%; EPS changed by less than one tenth of one percent. These are estimates and historical market prices from TECHi's data providers, not audited FY2027 results. Price adjustments were not confirmed by the quote page, and the estimate date's close is not necessarily the price at the exact moment the estimate was issued. The distinction matters because a valuation multiple is the market's willingness to pay for a dollar of forecast earnings. It can shrink when investors ask whether end customers will ultimately earn enough on AI to sustain infrastructure spending, even while current orders remain strong. Apollo's note gives that question a new data frame: it compares revenue per worker and profit margins for the seven biggest technology companies with the other 493 S&P 500 constituents and finds improvement concentrated in the tech group. Apollo also points to a productivity series and token-spending data. Its argument is about broad diffusion of AI benefits, not a census of every business using Nvidia hardware. Apollo's language is forceful, but the evidence supports a narrower investor conclusion than "AI demand has ended." Flat aggregate margins outside big tech cannot identify which individual firms used AI, when they adopted it, what they paid, or whether a particular project saved costs. A benefit can also arrive with a lag or be competed away in lower prices. The S&P 493 comparison is a reason to scrutinize the next layer of spending and pricing; it is not proof that Nvidia's next reported quarter will miss guidance. Nvidia's own August 26 results provide the counterweight. Revenue for the quarter ended July 26 was $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier. Data Center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117%. Using the more precise figures in its Form 10-Q, Data Center supplied about 92.5% of total quarterly revenue: $89.023 billion divided by $96.221 billion. This is a company whose current sales are deeply tied to the AI buildout, regardless of what Apollo's economy-wide charts say about customers' current returns. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point. The revenue midpoint is about 12.2% above the July quarter's $96.221 billion. Guidance is a management forecast, not a result. Nvidia specifically excluded Data Center compute revenue from China in that outlook. A quarter near the midpoint would show that equipment demand remained robust through the reporting period, though it would not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns. The route from enterprise budgets to Nvidia revenue is indirect. Nvidia sells to manufacturers, integrators, cloud providers, AI labs and others; a business can rent computing from a cloud provider rather than purchase Nvidia systems itself. The 10-Q says one direct customer accounted for 16% of second-quarter revenue. Nvidia also estimates that one AI research and deployment company contributed a meaningful amount of revenue by purchasing cloud services from its customers. It does not name that indirect customer in this disclosure. Investor exposure therefore depends on a chain of customers' funding, utilization and pricing decisions, not a single chart of non-tech corporate margins. There is a plausible delay between Apollo's concern and a chipmaker's results. Hyperscalers may continue building capacity already ordered or contracted even if some enterprise customers are still testing applications. AI labs may use more compute to train and serve models before the broader economy shows a productivity gain. Conversely, a long spell of poor downstream returns can eventually limit customers' willingness to pay, weaken cloud pricing and slow the next round of equipment orders. The investment question is the timing and strength of that feedback loop. Friday's $210.96 regular-session close on October 23 is the price baseline; US shares do not trade in their regular session on Saturday. TECHi's earnings calendar lists November 17, 2026 after market close as the next confirmed Nvidia report. The following are TECHi valuation sensitivities around that event, not analyst targets, probabilities, or a claim that these prices will trade on November 18. Each calculation starts from the October 24 FY2027 EPS estimate of $9.3124 shown on TECHi's forecast page and changes only the multiple. Results are rounded to cents after multiplication. The spread between $167.62 and $242.12 is $74.50 per share with the EPS input held fixed. That width shows how sensitive an expensive growth stock can be to the narrative about future demand. It does not measure expected volatility or substitute for an options market estimate. TECHi's live forecast page displays a mean analyst target of $328.95, but that target has an unspecified horizon and target sample count; it is neither a November target nor the source of our three cases. A more direct way to read the model is to ask what multiple the market assigns after seeing the next report. If Nvidia reports near its $108 billion revenue midpoint and around the guided 74% gross margin, investors could still refuse to restore September's 24.13-times multiple if downstream ROI remains uncertain. At the current $9.3124 estimate, 24.13 times would imply roughly $224.72, about 6.5% above Friday's close. That is the amount of valuation recovery required merely to revisit September's multiple using today's slightly higher EPS estimate. The earnings report can change the EPS input as well, so this calculation should not be read as a price target. Apollo's research is most useful as a testable warning. The bearish feedback loop would become more persuasive if cloud providers reported weaker AI-service pricing or utilization, if large buyers deferred infrastructure commitments, or if Nvidia's own guidance and gross margin fell below its August outlook. A broad-market productivity chart alone would not establish any of those company-specific developments. Nvidia's filings also identify power availability, land, capital and deployment constraints as reasons customers may postpone purchases; even healthy end demand could be delayed by physical infrastructure. The bullish counterargument is substantial. Nvidia has already shown extraordinary reported revenue growth, a 75% July-quarter gross margin, and a $108 billion next-quarter revenue midpoint. Management expects to sell both Blackwell and Rubin systems and says supply constraints remain. Demand can stay ahead of supply for a time even when average enterprise ROI is unclear. Strong cloud contracts, better utilization and pricing, or profitable deployment by customers would weaken Apollo's concern and support a higher multiple. None of those outcomes can be inferred from share-price movement alone. There is also a risk of measuring the wrong end of the chain. Apollo's S&P 493 series asks whether ordinary listed companies are seeing higher revenue per employee or margins. Nvidia's near-term customers include cloud and AI firms that may sell capacity to startups and enterprises worldwide. The public S&P 493 is not the full set of Nvidia's end users. Its companies also differ in accounting, sector mix and spending cycles. Treat Apollo's aggregate result as a challenge to the long-run AI demand thesis, not a substitute for Nvidia's reported sales or the next round of customer disclosures. For a holder deciding what to watch next, the order is practical. The October 26 market open will show how investors first price Apollo's dated research after the weekend; there is no Saturday regular-session NVDA move to report. Then the November 17 earnings release will test the $108 billion revenue midpoint, the 74% gross-margin guide, and management's comments on customer mix and capacity. Afterward, updates from the large cloud buyers will help determine whether rented AI compute is turning into durable, profitable demand. The forecast changes if those observations move the EPS estimate or justify a different multiple. Until then, the most defensible reading is that Nvidia's earnings expectations have held up far better than its valuation since late September.
